usage: 바뀌다 = something changes on its own / gets switched. The thing that changes takes 이/가, not 을/를.
The traffic light changed to green.
Use ~(으)로 바뀌다 for 'change INTO': 초록불로, 다른 걸로, 평일로.
examples: 회의 시간이 3시로 바뀌었어요.
The meeting time got changed to 3 o'clock.
Super common at work — schedules, plans, and times 'get changed' on you.
가게 이름이 바뀌었네요.
Oh, the shop's name changed.
~네요 adds a 'huh, I just noticed' tone — natural when you spot a change.
계획이 또 바뀔 수도 있어요.
The plan might change again.
또 (again) + 바뀌다 is the everyday way to warn that things aren't fixed yet.
nuance: 바뀌다 is the intransitive partner of 바꾸다 — the thing that changes is the subject (이/가), and no one is named as the one doing it. Use 바꾸다 when YOU actively swap something (번호를 바꿨어요), and 바뀌다 when it simply ends up different (번호가 바뀌었어요). Spelling matters: it's 바뀌- (with 위), and the polite form is 바뀌어요, not 바껴요.
mistakes: Don't use 바뀌다 transitively — you can't say '번호를 바뀌었어요'. If YOU did it, use 바꾸다: 번호를 바꿨어요.
Don't write the polite form as 바껴요; the standard form is 바뀌어요 (the 바뀌- stem doesn't contract to 바껴-).

usage: 달라지다 = end up noticeably different from before. Built from 다르다 (to be different) + 아/어지다.
뭐가 달라졌어요? is the natural way to ask 'what's different?' about a haircut, a room, etc.
examples: 머리 잘랐어요? 느낌이 달라졌네요.
Did you cut your hair? You look different.
Great compliment-ish line — 느낌이 달라졌다 = the vibe/impression changed.
살아 보니까 생각이 많이 달라졌어요.
Living here, my way of thinking has changed a lot.
Use for gradual inner change — 생각이/가치관이 달라지다.
내년부터 규정이 달라질 거예요.
The rules will be different starting next year.
Common in notices about policies, fees, or schedules changing.
nuance: 달라지다 emphasizes that the result is now different from how it was, so it's the go-to verb for noticing change in someone's looks, mood, or a situation. It overlaps with 변하다 (to change), but 달라지다 feels more about the visible before-and-after gap, while 변하다 leans toward a thing transforming over time. Both are intransitive: the changed thing takes 이/가.
mistakes: Don't confuse it with 다르다 (to be different) — 다르다 describes a static difference (A는 B와 달라요), while 달라지다 describes the act of becoming different (분위기가 달라졌어요).
It's intransitive, so don't attach 을/를: say 생각이 달라졌어요, not 생각을 달라졌어요.

english: to increase, to grow, to stretch out
usage: My workload has grown a lot lately.
늘어나다 = an amount/number gets bigger. Slightly more vivid than plain 늘다.
The T-shirt stretched out after I washed it.
Also the everyday word for clothes losing shape — 옷이 늘어나다. 빨다 is transitive, so the shirt takes 를 here.
examples: 외국인 주민이 점점 늘어나고 있어요.
The foreign resident population keeps growing.
점점 + 늘어나고 있어요 = 'is gradually increasing' — common in news and small talk.
카드값이 갑자기 늘어났어요.
My card bill suddenly went up.
Money talk: 지출이/요금이 늘어나다 (expenses/fees increase).
연습하면 단어가 자연스럽게 늘어날 거예요.
If you practice, your vocabulary will naturally grow.
Encouraging line about skills/knowledge increasing.
nuance: 늘어나다 means a quantity, number, or length gets bigger, and it feels a touch more concrete and visual than 늘다 — picture something physically stretching or a count climbing. It's intransitive (the thing that grows takes 이/가); if YOU increase something on purpose, use the transitive 늘리다 (시간을 늘리다). For clothes and elastic things, 늘어나다 also means to stretch out and lose shape.
mistakes: Don't pair it with 을/를 as if it were transitive — say 일이 늘어났어요, not 일을 늘어났어요. Use 늘리다 when you actively increase something.
Don't confuse 늘어나다 (to increase) with 늘어서다 (to line up in a row); they look similar but mean different things.

english: to decrease, to shrink, to dwindle
usage: My stress has gone down a lot.
줄어들다 = an amount/number gets smaller. More vivid than plain 줄다.
My account balance is dropping fast.
examples: 손님이 갑자기 줄어들었어요.
Customers suddenly dropped off.
Business small talk — 손님이/매출이 줄어들다.
체중이 조금씩 줄어들고 있어요.
My weight is gradually going down.
조금씩 + 줄어들고 있어요 = 'is decreasing little by little'.
월세 싼 데로 옮기면 부담이 줄어들 거예요.
If you move to a place with cheaper rent, the burden will lessen.
부담이 줄어들다 = the (financial/mental) burden eases. 옮기다 takes a place, not the rent itself.
nuance: 줄어들다 means a quantity, size, or pressure shrinks, and it's a touch more vivid and gradual-feeling than plain 줄다. It's a ㄹ-stem verb, so the final ㄹ drops before -ㅂ니다 and -(으) endings: 줄어듭니다, 줄어드세요. It's intransitive — the thing that shrinks takes 이/가; when YOU reduce something on purpose, use the transitive 줄이다 (소리를 줄이다, 양을 줄이다).
mistakes: Don't write the formal form as 줄어들습니다 — the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, so it's 줄어듭니다.
Don't use it transitively: say 비용이 줄어들었어요 (the cost decreased), but 비용을 줄였어요 (I reduced the cost) with 줄이다.

usage: 사라지다 = something is gone / no longer there. The lost thing takes 이/가.
거짓말처럼 사라지다 ('disappear like a lie') is a common, vivid set phrase for symptoms easing.
examples: 저장한 파일이 다 사라졌어요.
All my saved files disappeared.
Tech panic line — 데이터가/파일이 사라지다.
그 카페는 1년 만에 사라졌어요.
That cafe was gone within a year.
Used for shops/places closing down and vanishing from the neighborhood.
걱정이 곧 사라질 거예요.
Your worries will soon disappear.
Comforting — abstract things (걱정, 불안) can 사라지다 too.
nuance: 사라지다 means something stops being present — it's gone from sight or existence — and works for objects, people, places, and even feelings like worry or pain. It's intransitive and a bit more dramatic than 없어지다, often carrying a sense of vanishing suddenly or completely. The thing that disappears is the subject (이/가); there's no one 'doing' the disappearing.
mistakes: Don't use it transitively — you can't 'disappear something'. To make something gone, use 없애다 (없애 주세요) or 지우다 (delete).
Don't confuse 사라지다 (to vanish) with 사다 (to buy) — they only look similar at the start.

english: to come up, to arise, to form, to get
usage: 일이 생기다 = something (an errand/issue) comes up — the #1 polite excuse for canceling plans.
A convenience store opened in front of my place.
생기다 = come into existence / appear. Used when a new shop, building, or thing shows up.
examples: 여드름이 또 생겼어요.
I got another pimple.
For skin issues, bruises, etc.: 여드름이/멍이 생기다 ('a pimple/bruise forms').
남자친구 생겼어요?
Did you get a boyfriend?
Casual but super common — 애인이/여자친구가 생기다 = 'to get a partner'.
문제가 생기면 바로 연락 주세요.
If a problem comes up, contact me right away.
문제가 생기다 = a problem arises; the conditional 생기면 is everyday phrasing.
nuance: 생기다 covers a wide range: something coming into existence (가게가 생기다), an event/issue arising (일이/문제가 생기다), or a person 'getting' something they didn't have before (돈이/시간이/애인이 생기다). It's intransitive even when English says 'get' — the thing you acquire takes 이/가, not 을/를. Separately, 생기다 can mean 'to look (a certain way)': 잘생기다 = good-looking.
mistakes: Don't translate 'I got X' with 을/를 — it's 시간이 생겼어요 (I got time), not 시간을 생겼어요.
When canceling plans, '일이 생겼어요' is the natural excuse; learners often over-explain instead of using this set phrase.

english: to break down, to get ruined
usage: My umbrella got wrecked by the wind.
망가지다 = something breaks and stops working / loses its shape. The broken thing takes 이/가.
For appliances/gadgets failing; close to 고장나다 but often implies more physical damage.
examples: 택배 상자가 다 망가진 채로 왔어요.
The parcel box arrived completely wrecked.
~ㄴ 채로 = 'in a (ruined) state'; useful for complaints to delivery/sellers.
비 맞아서 신발이 망가졌어요.
My shoes got ruined from the rain.
Everyday for clothes/shoes/bags getting damaged beyond use.
다이어트 계획이 완전히 망가졌어요.
My diet plan totally fell apart.
Figurative — plans, routines, or moods can 망가지다 ('get wrecked').
nuance: 망가지다 means something is damaged to the point it no longer works or holds its shape — broader than 고장나다 (which is mainly about machines failing). It covers appliances, physical objects, and figuratively plans, health, or routines that fall apart. It's intransitive; when a person ruins something on purpose, use the transitive 망가뜨리다 or 망치다.
mistakes: Don't use it transitively — say 핸드폰이 망가졌어요 (the phone broke), but 핸드폰을 망가뜨렸어요 / 망쳤어요 when YOU broke it.
For pure machine malfunction, 고장났어요 is often more natural; reserve 망가지다 when there's real physical damage or 'wreckage'.

english: to collapse, to crumble, to fall apart
usage: 무너지다 = a structure caves in / crumbles down. The thing that collapses takes 이/가.
멘탈이 무너지다 is super common slang among 20–30s for 'I lost it / I broke down'.
examples: 폭우로 다리가 무너졌어요.
The bridge collapsed in the heavy rain.
Disaster/news context — 건물이/다리가 무너지다.
계획이 한순간에 무너졌어요.
My plans collapsed in an instant.
Figurative — plans, dreams, or systems 'falling apart'.
그 소식에 마음이 무너졌어요.
My heart sank at that news.
마음이 무너지다 = to be emotionally crushed; very natural and a bit literary.
nuance: 무너지다 literally means a structure crumbles or caves in (a wall, building, bridge), but it's used just as often figuratively for emotions, plans, or order collapsing. Among younger Koreans, 멘탈이 무너지다 ('my mental collapsed') is everyday slang for breaking down under stress. It's intransitive; to knock something down on purpose, use 무너뜨리다.
mistakes: Don't use it transitively — say 건물이 무너졌어요 (the building collapsed), but 건물을 무너뜨렸어요 when something/someone brought it down.
Don't confuse the emotional 마음이 무너지다 (heart breaks) with mild disappointment; it's strong, for genuinely crushing moments.

english: to break, to shatter, to fall through
usage: 깨지다 = a hard/brittle thing shatters or cracks. The broken thing takes 이/가.
액정이 깨지다 is the standard way to say your phone screen is broken/cracked.
examples: 계란이 가방 안에서 깨졌어요.
The eggs broke inside my bag.
For brittle things — 유리가/접시가/계란이 깨지다.
약속이 깨졌어요.
The plans fell through.
Figurative — 약속이/계약이 깨지다 = a promise/deal falls apart.
둘이 결국 깨졌어요.
The two of them broke up in the end.
Casual slang: 깨지다 = to break up (a couple), like 헤어지다.
nuance: 깨지다 is for hard, brittle things shattering or cracking — glass, dishes, phone screens, eggs — as opposed to 부러지다 (long things snapping) or 찢어지다 (paper/fabric tearing). Figuratively it covers promises, deals, or records 'breaking' (기록이 깨지다), and in casual speech it means a couple breaking up. It's intransitive; to smash something yourself, use the transitive 깨다 (컵을 깼어요).
mistakes: Don't use it transitively — say 유리가 깨졌어요 (the glass broke), but 유리를 깼어요 when YOU broke it (깨다).
Match the verb to the material: glass/ceramics 깨지다, sticks/bones 부러지다, paper/clothes 찢어지다.

english: to burst, to explode, to go off
usage: 터지다 = (signal) comes through. 와이파이/인터넷/데이터가 터지다 is the everyday way to say a signal works.
The balloon popped with a bang.
Core meaning: something bursts/explodes. 펑 is the popping sound effect.
examples: 여기 지하라서 폰이 안 터져요.
It's a basement, so my phone has no signal.
폰이 안 터지다 = 'no reception' — essential for cafes, subways, basements.
물집이 터져서 아파요.
My blister popped and it hurts.
For body stuff — 물집이/혈관이 터지다.
참다가 결국 화가 터졌어요.
I held it in but my anger finally exploded.
화가 터지다 = anger erupts; also 웃음이 터지다 = to burst out laughing.
nuance: 터지다 literally means to burst or explode (balloons, blisters, pipes), but two everyday uses dominate daily life in Korea: signal coverage (와이파이/폰이 터지다 = the signal works) and emotions erupting (화가/웃음이/울음이 터지다). It's intransitive; to set something off or pop it yourself, use the transitive 터뜨리다 (풍선을 터뜨리다).
mistakes: For phone reception, '안 터져요' means 'no signal' — don't say 안 돼요, which is vaguer.
Don't use it transitively — say 풍선이 터졌어요 (the balloon popped), but 풍선을 터뜨렸어요 when YOU popped it.

usage: 멎다 = a flowing/ongoing natural thing ceases on its own. The thing that stops takes 이/가.
examples: 눈이 멎으면 나갈게요.
I'll head out once the snow stops.
Conditional 멎으면 = 'once it stops' — natural for weather.
놀라서 심장이 멎는 줄 알았어요.
I was so startled my heart felt like it stopped.
심장이 멎다 = heart stops; the set phrase 멎는 줄 알았어요 = 'I thought it would stop'.
한참 뒤에야 빗소리가 멎었어요.
The sound of rain stopped only after a long while.
Slightly literary; 멎다 has a quieter, more natural feel than 멈추다.
nuance: 멎다 means something flowing or continuous comes to a halt by itself — rain, snow, bleeding, a heartbeat. It overlaps with 멈추다 (to stop), but 멎다 is narrower and a bit more literary, reserved for natural or bodily processes rather than machines or vehicles. It's intransitive and never takes an object; for stopping a car or a machine you'd use 멈추다 or 세우다.
mistakes: Don't use 멎다 for vehicles or machines — say 차가 멈췄어요 (the car stopped), not 차가 멎었어요.
It's intransitive, so don't add 을/를: 피가 멎었어요 (the bleeding stopped), not 피를 멎었어요.

english: to continue, to be connected, to lead to
usage: This road leads to the market.
이어지다 = one thing connects/continues to another. Often with ~(으)로 (leads to) or 까지 (continues until).
Use for things that continue without a break — 분위기가/대화가/날씨가 이어지다.
examples: 더위가 다음 주까지 이어질 거예요.
The heat will continue into next week.
Weather forecasts love this — 폭염이/장마가 이어지다.
작은 습관이 큰 변화로 이어져요.
Small habits lead to big change.
~(으)로 이어지다 = 'leads to (a result)'; great for advice/motivation.
회의가 저녁까지 이어졌어요.
The meeting dragged on until evening.
이어지다 = an event runs on longer than expected, without stopping.
nuance: 이어지다 means something continues without breaking, or one thing connects into another — a road leading somewhere, weather persisting, a conversation flowing on, or a cause leading to a result (X로 이어지다). It's the intransitive partner of 잇다 (to connect/join); when you actively link things, use 잇다 or 이어 가다 (전통을 이어 가다 = to carry on a tradition). The connected thing takes 이/가.
mistakes: Don't use it transitively — say 대화가 이어졌어요 (the conversation continued), but 대화를 이어 갔어요 when someone keeps it going (이어 가다).
For 'leads to a result,' use the particle (으)로: 노력이 성공으로 이어졌어요, not 성공에 이어졌어요.
